before: Array.indexOf(value) returns the first matching index or -1. For the string arrays in this lesson it finds exact matching text. A missing value must be handled before splice: using index -1 would target the last element rather than do nothing.

array.splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) removes deleteCount elements at start and inserts any supplied items there. It mutates that array and returns a new array of the removed elements. To preserve a caller’s source, first make a shallow copy with slice().

forEach(callback) calls the callback for each present element and returns undefined. A callback’s returned values are ignored; use map when you want a result array. The example uses forEach to accumulate a total only as a clear side-effect demonstration.

replaceFirst(values, oldValue, newValue) copies the input string array, finds its first exact oldValue, replaces that one entry if found, and returns the copy. Leave later duplicates unchanged and never remove the final entry on a miss. JSON.stringify(value) formats these simple arrays/objects as JSON text for display; it returns a string and does not edit the value.
Implement replaceFirst for string arrays. Preserve the original, replace only the first exact match, and return a distinct copy even if no match exists.
after:
`indexOf(value)` gives the first matching position, or -1 if it finds none. Here, the entries are strings and must match exactly.

Check for -1 before editing. For `splice`, -1 means the last item, not “nothing found.”

`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` removes items and puts new ones in their place. It changes the array and returns an array of the removed items.

Make a copy with `slice()` first when the original must stay unchanged. That copy is shallow: nested objects would still be shared.

`forEach` calls a function for each existing item, then returns `undefined`. It ignores the callback's returned answers.

Use `map` to build an array of answers. The example uses `forEach` only to show changing a running total.

`replaceFirst` copies the array, searches for `oldValue`, and replaces only the first match. A missing value leaves the copy's contents alone.

`JSON.stringify` turns these simple arrays into text so you can see their contents.
Return a new array even when no item matches. Keep later duplicates and every original input value unchanged.
